Learning notes: Paper Trade Crude Oil WTI (WTI)

Simulate buying and selling Crude Oil WTI (WTI) with $100,000 in virtual cash. Charts and prices are for education only — no real money, no brokerage relationship.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

What Crude Oil WTI is

West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is a crude-oil benchmark. Oil is refined into petroleum products, and supply, inventories, refining and consumption are different parts of its market. TradeHQ uses a simplified WTI-labelled practice instrument and does not execute a deliverable oil contract.

Reference facts
Asset Class: Commodity
Benchmark: WTI
Units: Barrels
How to practise it here

Analyze price action around OPEC+ meetings, EIA inventory reports, and geopolitical tensions. Practice understanding supply-demand dynamics. (Educational simulation only — not financial advice.)

Asset-specific worksheet (hypothetical)

Draw a chain from crude production to refining to fuel consumption. Put a hypothetical refinery outage and a production cut at their different points in the chain. Explain why the same word, oil, can obscure different prices and physical constraints.

Why learners study Crude Oil WTI

Crude oil is a global commodity whose price affects inflation, transport costs and the profits of entire sectors. It is a good market for learning how supply news drives price.

What tends to move Crude Oil WTI

OPEC+ production decisions, weekly inventory reports, geopolitical events in producing regions and global demand forecasts are the drivers covered most often.

Crude Oil WTI: practice versus a real account

Most real oil trading uses futures contracts that expire and must be rolled, and those contracts carry leverage. The simulator's simple price hides that complexity.

Common questions about trading Crude Oil WTI
How to practice crude oil trading for free? — TradeHQ provides a WTI-labelled spot practice instrument with $100K virtual cash. Inventory reports and OPEC+ decisions are study topics; this simulator does not execute oil futures or reproduce actual news reactions.
What factors can affect crude oil prices? — OPEC+ production decisions, inventory data, geopolitical events and global demand expectations are among the factors that can affect oil prices. Their effects can overlap or be offset by other developments.
Is oil useful for a beginner practice exercise? — Oil can illustrate how commodity prices respond to supply, demand and news. A learner can compare hypothetical position sizes with virtual cash; this does not establish that oil is suitable for a real-money beginner account.
How can geopolitical events affect oil prices? — Conflict, sanctions and shipping disruptions can alter supply expectations and coincide with sharp oil moves, but the magnitude and direction are not guaranteed. Use historical examples as observations rather than trading instructions.
A practice checklist for Crude Oil WTI
Check the date of the next OPEC+ meeting.
Note whether a weekly inventory report is due during your holding period.
Compare chosen price shocks and hypothetical exposures; futures margin and automatic stops are not implemented here.
Read the Crude Oil WTI sections above and look up any term here you cannot define out loud. Educational simulation only — not financial advice.
